title: Skimming, Scanning & Time Management
summary: Sixty minutes, roughly 2,700 words to read, forty answers to write, and no transfer time — you cannot read every word and still finish. This lesson teaches the three reading gears IELTS actually rewards: skim for shape, scan to locate, read closely only for the sentence that answers the question.

seo.title: IELTS Reading: Skimming, Scanning & Timing | GrowQR
seo.description: Skim, scan and manage time in IELTS Reading. Read for the gist, locate answers fast, guess vocabulary in context and never lose marks to the clock.

objectives: Skim a passage for its structure and general idea in about two minutes
Scan to locate a specific word, name, date or number without reading in full
Guess the meaning of unknown vocabulary from surrounding context
Follow a 20-minute-per-passage plan and a 90-second decide-and-move rule

blocks.html:
The mistake almost every new IELTS candidate makes is treating the Reading test like a school comprehension exercise: read the whole passage carefully, understand it fully, then answer the questions. Try that here and you will run out of time somewhere in Passage 2, with Passage 3 — the hardest and just as many marks — barely touched. There simply isn't time to read three long passages word by word and answer forty questions and write them on the sheet, all inside sixty minutes with no time added for transfer.

Skilled test-takers don't read faster. They read differently, switching between three gears depending on what the moment needs. This applies equally to Academic and General Training — the passages differ, the technique doesn't.

The three gears

Every effective reader in an exam uses three distinct modes, and knowing which one you're in is half the skill.

  • Skimming — fast reading for the general idea and structure. You're building a mental map: what is this about, how is it organised, where does each part live? You do this once, at the start, in a couple of minutes.
  • Scanning — moving your eyes quickly over the text to locate a specific thing: a name, a date, a number, a keyword. You're not reading for meaning here; you're searching, the way you'd hunt for a friend's name in a list.
  • Reading in detail — slow, careful reading of the one or two sentences that actually answer a question, once scanning has found them.

SkimmingScanningDetailed reading
GoalGrasp the gist and structureFind a specific piece of informationWork out the exact answer
SpeedFastVery fastSlow and careful
What you readTitle, first & last paragraphs, first sentence of each paragraphYou look for a target — name, number, keyword — ignoring everything elseOnly the sentence(s) around the answer
WhenOnce, before the questionsFor each question, to find the right linesAfter scanning has located the lines
Question types it servesMatching Headings, main-idea questionsCompletion, matching information, most detail questionsTrue/False/Not Given, multiple choice

How to skim well

Skimming isn't reading quickly and hoping some of it sticks. It's targeted. When you first meet a passage, read the title and any subheading, the whole first paragraph and the whole last paragraph, and then the first sentence of every paragraph in between. Writers put the point of a paragraph in its opening sentence far more often than not, so this handful of lines tells you what each paragraph is for. Spend about two minutes on this and don't stop for words you don't know — you're after the shape, not the detail.

The payoff comes later. When a question asks about, say, the cost of a project, your skim has already told you "paragraph D is the money paragraph", so you scan D instead of the whole text.

blocks.title: Scanning to find an answer fast
items: Pull a target out of the question. Pick the most searchable word — a proper noun, a year, a figure, a technical term. These are the easiest things to spot on a page.
Sweep, don't read. Run your eyes down the text looking only for that target. Capitalised names, dates and numbers physically stand out, so let them jump at you.
Use passage order. Most question sets run in the order of the text, so the next answer is usually below the last one — start scanning from where you just were.
Switch to detailed reading once you land. When you hit the target, slow right down and read the sentence — and often the one before and after — carefully to settle the answer.

blocks.title: Names, dates and numbers are your friends
blocks.html: Capital letters and digits are the easiest things for the eye to catch, which makes questions containing a name ("Dr Halvorsen"), a year ("1998") or a figure ("12 per cent") the fastest to locate. Start your scan from the most distinctive item in the question, then read the surrounding sentence for the actual answer.

You don't need to understand every word

Here's a liberating truth that panicked candidates forget: you will not know every word in the passage, and you don't need to. IELTS passages are chosen to contain vocabulary beyond your comfort zone. Stopping dead at each unfamiliar word is how people run out of time. Instead, read on — the meaning of an unknown word is usually recoverable from the words around it. This skill, vocabulary in context, is worth practising deliberately because it saves you both time and nerve.

blocks.title: Guessing a word from context
blocks.html: Take this sentence: "The desert plants are remarkably xerophytic, surviving months without rain by storing water in their thick, waxy leaves." You may never have seen "xerophytic", and you don't have to. The rest of the sentence — surviving without rain, storing water — tells you it means something like "drought-resistant". That's more than enough to answer a question. Look for definitions, examples, contrasts ("unlike…") and the general drift of the sentence, and keep moving.

The clock is the real examiner

Reading technique only matters if it's harnessed to a plan. With three passages in sixty minutes, the arithmetic is simple: about 20 minutes per passage, questions and answer-writing included. And because there is no transfer time, you write each answer on the answer sheet as you go — not in a heroic dash at the end, which is how candidates routinely lose eight or ten answers when the clock beats them.

blocks.title: A 60-minute plan that leaves nothing blank
items: Passage 1 — about 20 minutes. On General Training this is the easiest text; bank the marks and, if you can, finish a little early to buy time for later.
Passage 2 — about 20 minutes. Difficulty steps up. Keep the same skim-scan-read rhythm and don't let one stubborn question eat your budget.
Passage 3 — about 20 minutes. The hardest passage carries just as many marks as the first. Protect this time fiercely; never let Passages 1 and 2 overrun into it.
Write answers on the sheet as you go. With no transfer time, every answer goes straight onto the sheet the moment you decide it.
Final sweep for blanks. There's no penalty for a wrong answer, so fill every gap with a best guess before time is called — a blank can never score.

blocks.title: The 90-second rule: decide and move
blocks.html: Never spend more than about 90 seconds stuck on a single question. One question is worth exactly one mark — the same as an easy one you haven't reached yet. When a question resists, write your best guess, flag it, and move on. You can return with spare time at the end, but you can never get back the four minutes you burned staring at it. Guarding your time is worth more marks than solving any one hard question.

Putting the gears together

A full pass on a passage looks like this: skim for two minutes to build the map, read the questions, then for each question scan to the right lines and read those lines closely — writing each answer down as you go, guessing unknown words from context, and moving on the moment 90 seconds are up. Do that three times, keep to 20 minutes a passage, and you finish with every answer filled in.

Time to test the whole system on a real passage. Start with the Academic practice set or, if you're sitting the other version, the General Training set. For official free practice material, see IELTS, the British Council and IDP.

faqs.q: What is the difference between skimming and scanning in IELTS Reading?
faqs.a: Skimming is fast reading for the general idea and structure — you read the title, the first and last paragraphs, and the first sentence of each paragraph. Scanning is moving your eyes quickly to locate one specific thing, such as a name, date or number, without reading for meaning.

faqs.q: Do I need to understand every word in an IELTS Reading passage?
faqs.a: No. Passages are deliberately chosen to include unfamiliar vocabulary, and stopping at every unknown word wastes time. Guess the meaning from the surrounding context and keep reading — the sentence around a word usually reveals enough to answer the question.

faqs.q: How much time should I spend on each reading passage?
faqs.a: About 20 minutes per passage, which must include reading, answering and writing your answers on the sheet. There is no extra transfer time, so write each answer as you go rather than saving it for the end.

faqs.q: What should I do when I get stuck on a question?
faqs.a: Follow the 90-second rule: never spend more than about a minute and a half on one question. Write your best guess, flag it, and move on — every question is worth one mark, and there is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.
